outline.description: This chapter covers the events leading to the case, including the 911 call, the officer's interactions with Lisa Coleman at the home, the critical exchange that formed the basis for consent, what the officers discovered upon entry, and the procedural path from indictment through the suppression hearing to the conditional plea and appeal.
subtopics: The 911 domestic violence call and Officer Kizer's arrival at the Coleman home
Lisa's initial responses and her first refusal of entry
The critical second exchange: Officer Kizer's statement of need and Lisa's consent
The officers' entry, their actions inside the home, and discovery of information from the children
The search warrant, recovery of firearms, and federal indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)
Coleman's motion to suppress, the magistrate judge's report, and the district court's ruling
The conditional guilty plea preserving the right to appeal the suppression ruling

outline.chapter_title: Legal Framework: The Fourth Amendment Consent Doctrine
outline.description: This chapter explains the governing legal principles the court applied, including consent as an exception to the warrant requirement, third-party consent under Matlock, the voluntariness standard, the totality-of-the-circumstances test and its factors, the objective reasonableness standard for scope of consent, and the clear-error standard of appellate review.
subtopics: Consent as a well-established exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement
Third-party consent: a person with common authority may consent to search shared premises (Matlock doctrine)
The voluntariness requirement: consent must be freely and voluntarily given (Bumper v. North Carolina)
The totality-of-the-circumstances test and the six illustrative voluntariness factors
Scope of consent evaluated under an objective reasonableness standard (Florida v. Jimeno)
The role of body camera footage in resolving factual disputes about consent
Standard of review: clear error for findings of voluntary consent and scope

outline.chapter_title: Applying the Voluntariness Standard to Lisa's Consent
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the court's application of the voluntariness factors to the interaction between Officer Kizer and Lisa, focusing on why the court found consent was voluntary despite Coleman's argument that the officer's use of the word 'need' rendered the encounter coercive.
subtopics: Officer Kizer's tone and demeanor: concerned rather than coercive
Lisa's demonstrated capacity to refuse consent, evidenced by her initial denial of entry
The significance of Officer Kizer asking for permission a second time without coercion
The brief duration of the encounter and Lisa's non-custodial status
Coleman's argument centered on the word 'need' and why the court found it too narrow
The totality-of-circumstances analysis supporting the district court's finding of voluntary consent
Lisa's responsive conduct confirming she understood the request as one for permission

outline.chapter_title: Scope of Consent, Alternative Theories, and Disposition
outline.description: This chapter examines whether the officers exceeded the scope of Lisa's consent once inside the home, the information that led to the warrant, the government's alternative theories that the court declined to reach, and the court's final disposition and closing observations.
subtopics: The officers' stated purpose: checking the welfare of the children
Whether scanning the home, locating occupants, and asking basic questions fell within the scope of consent
The protective pat-down of Coleman and information gathered from the children
How information obtained during the entry led to the search warrant and recovery of firearms
The government's alternative arguments: exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery
Why the court declined to reach the alternative theories given its ruling on consent
The court's affirmance and closing observation on the officers' decision-making in difficult circumstances
